title: Inside Chinchilla: why 70B parameters beat 280B on the same compute
summary: Chinchilla upends the old rule that more compute means more parameters: model size and data should grow together, roughly 20 tokens per parameter. We unpack the learning-rate bias in the earlier experiments, the three estimation methods, the three-way loss decomposition, calculate an IsoFLOP valley by hand, and list the paper's internal inconsistencies and the new considerations raised by LLaMA.
ai_summary: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (DeepMind, 2022) trained over 400 models and used three methods to estimate the optimal allocation under a fixed compute budget. All three reached the same conclusion: model size and training data both scale roughly as the 0.5 power of compute, about 20 tokens per parameter, rather than Kaplan et al.'s 0.73 and 0.27. The difference stems mainly from the earlier experiments using a single learning-rate schedule for all models. A 70B-parameter Chinchilla trained under Gopher's compute budget on 1.4 trillion tokens reached 67.6% on MMLU, beating the 280B Gopher on almost every task. The paper contains many internal numeric inconsistencies; later, LLaMA factored in inference cost and chose smaller models trained longer.
brief: The question: with a fixed compute budget, how large should the model be and how much data should it see? At the time, large models kept adding parameters while training data stayed around 300 billion tokens.
The method: train over 400 models and estimate independently with three approaches: the training-curve lower envelope, IsoFLOP valleys, and a three-term loss decomposition.
The result: model size and data should grow together, about 20 tokens per parameter; 70B Chinchilla beats 280B Gopher with the same compute.
Limits: the main large-scale validation is only one pair of models, and it mixes in optimizer differences; inference cost is not considered, and many numbers are internally inconsistent.

paper.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
paper.authors: Jordan Hoffmann, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford and 16 others — 22 authors in total.

cover.headline: Chinchilla: a close read of the original paper
cover.highlight: Model and data should grow together

big.label: Training tokens per parameter at the compute-optimal point

blocks.p: In March 2022, 22 authors at DeepMind released this 36-page paper. It revisits the question from our previous close reading of Scaling Laws: **with a fixed compute budget, how large should the model be and how much data should it see?**

Two years earlier, OpenAI concluded that more compute should mostly go into a bigger model, with data growing only slowly. This paper reruns the experiments with over 400 models and reaches a very different answer: **model size and training data should scale in equal proportions** — each time the model doubles, the data should double too. By their estimate, at the compute-optimal point each parameter needs about 20 training tokens.

By that standard, the big models of the time were all underfed: GPT-3, Gopher, MT-NLG, and other 100B-plus models mostly trained on only about 300 billion tokens. To test this, the authors trained a model called Chinchilla with **exactly the same compute** as Gopher (280B parameters) but only 70B parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens. It beat Gopher on almost every benchmark, improving MMLU from 60.0% to 67.6%. Four times smaller, and much cheaper to use.

This paper changed how the industry trains large models. After it, teams stopped piling on parameters and instead pushed training data into the trillions of tokens; later, they even deliberately trained models longer than compute-optimal because a smaller model saves even more money at deployment.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: With a fixed compute budget, optimal model size N and training tokens D both scale roughly as the 0.5 power of compute: double the model, double the data, with about 20 tokens per parameter. Three independent estimation methods reach the same conclusion, and 70B Chinchilla beats 280B Gopher using the same compute.

callout.title: Four concepts you need
callout.text: If you are not familiar with them, these four are enough:
list: **Loss and power laws**: loss measures how badly the model guesses the next token; it falls as a power law of model size and data volume. See our close reading of Scaling Laws.
**Training compute ≈ 6ND**: training a model with N parameters on D tokens costs about 6 × N × D floating-point operations. So for a fixed compute budget, N and D trade off against each other.
**IsoFLOP**: "same compute." An IsoFLOP curve holds compute fixed and varies model size, with data changing accordingly, to see which combination achieves the lowest loss.
**Cosine learning-rate schedule**: the learning rate decreases gradually from a high value along a cosine curve. Its "cycle length" must be set in advance — the key detail in this paper.

sections.h: The problem: everyone added parameters, not data

blocks.p: In 2020, Scaling Laws recommended that a 10× increase in compute should grow the model about 5.5× but data only about 1.8× (the numbers as reported in this paper). Large models over the next two years largely followed this recipe: parameters rose from 175B to 530B while training data stayed almost flat at around 300 billion tokens:

fig.title: The largest models at the time: more parameters, data barely moved
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Table 1; "tokens per parameter" is computed by us. Amber is Chinchilla.

blocks.p: Why does this matter? The compute budget for training a large model is usually fixed in advance: how many accelerators you have and how long you can use them. And such models can usually only be trained once, so if the model size or training length is chosen badly, there is no second chance.

sections.h: Key finding: the earlier experiments hid a bias

blocks.p: The paper identifies a flaw in the experimental design of Scaling Laws: it used **the same training length and learning-rate schedule** for all models — a cosine decay to a fixed token count — then used mid-training loss to stand in for "what happens if I train on only this many tokens."

The problem is that a cosine schedule needs to complete a full cycle before a model "finishes," and the loss drops fastest at the end of the cycle. If the schedule is designed for 130B tokens, stopping at 20B tokens leaves the learning rate still high and the model unfinished, so the loss is higher than for a model trained with a schedule designed specifically for 20B tokens. As a result, training on less data was systematically underestimated, pushing the conclusion toward "more parameters, less data."

callout.title: Like timing a 10K using marathon pace
callout.text: A runner sets out at marathon pace, and you stop the clock at 10K. The time will be slower than if they had raced a 10K: they are saving energy and have not kicked. If you then conclude "this person is bad at short distances," you are doing them an injustice. The old experiments made exactly this mistake by using mid-training loss to represent short training runs.

blocks.p: The paper confirms this: if the cosine cycle is more than 25% longer than the actual training steps, the model visibly worsens. So every experiment in this paper sets the learning-rate cycle length to match the training length, with the learning rate decaying 10× over the run. Two other differences: this paper uses larger models, mostly above 500M parameters and up to 16B, while the old experiments were mostly much smaller, many under 100M. The paper also finds that the relationship between compute and optimal model size curves slightly at large scale, so extrapolating from small models introduces bias.

quiz.q: Why would measuring mid-training loss with a schedule designed for a long training run make people underestimate the value of training on less data?
options: Because mid-training measurements are noisier
Because the learning-rate cycle has not completed, the model has not "finished," and mid-training loss is higher than for a model trained specifically to that length
Because the model has fewer parameters mid-training
Because the model has not seen the test set yet
quiz.why: A cosine schedule lowers the learning rate in the final phase, and that is when loss drops fastest. Stopping mid-training leaves the learning rate high and the loss elevated. Treating that as "the level achievable with this much data" overestimates the loss for training on less data, and so underestimates its value. The parameter count does not change during training, and the test set is irrelevant to training progress.

sections.h: Method 1: draw the lower envelope of all training curves

blocks.p: The first method is the most direct. Take a set of models from 70M to over 10B parameters, and train each size four times, with learning-rate cycles set for four different training lengths, the longest and shortest differing by a factor of 16. Plot all training curves on a compute–loss chart, then for each compute value find which curve has the lowest loss and record its model size and the number of tokens it has seen.

callout.title: What is the lower envelope?
callout.text: Take dozens of training curves sloping from upper left to lower right, stack them together, and trace along the bottom. That line is "the lowest loss achievable at each compute level." Each point on it corresponds to a specific model size and data volume — the optimal combination for that compute budget.

blocks.p: After sampling 1,500 logarithmically spaced compute values, they fit power laws for how optimal model size and optimal token count scale with compute: N_{opt} ∝ C^{a}, D_{opt} ∝ C^{b}. The result is **a = 0.50 and b = 0.50**: the two grow exactly in lockstep. The paper also notes that the chosen points all fall within the last 15% of their training runs — another sign that the learning-rate cycle must match training length.

sections.h: Method 2: fix compute and find the loss "valley"

blocks.p: The second method is more intuitive. Pick nine compute budgets from 6 × 10^{18} to 3 × 10^{21} FLOPs, and for each budget train a range of model sizes: the larger the model, the fewer tokens it sees, exactly using up the budget. Then look at how final loss depends on model size.

For every budget, the loss forms a clear valley: too small a model cannot absorb the knowledge; too large a model gets too little data and is undertrained. The valley floor is the optimal model for that budget. The paper fits a parabola to each curve to locate the floor, then fits a power law through the floors, giving **a = 0.49 and b = 0.51**.

fig.title: Same Gopher compute, different splits: the middle wins, both extremes lag
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: computed by us from the paper's Method 3 fitted formula and rounded parameters, using compute of 5.76 × 10^{23} and D = C / 6N. Not measured data. Amber marks the valley floor.
fig.note: The valley is fairly flat: from 20B to 70B the differences are small, but 280B is clearly worse. With rounded parameters, the valley floor is around 32B; the paper uses unrounded parameters and gets about 40B. The "predicted loss" also includes an irreducible constant of 1.69, explained in Method 3 below.

plain.title: Fixed budget, find the valley
plain.text: Compute is fixed: make the model bigger and it sees less data; make it smaller and it can see more. Connect the losses of all these splits and you get a valley curve that falls then rises. Models near the valley floor are much smaller than Gopher, the point on the right, yet achieve lower loss.

quiz.q: On an IsoFLOP curve, why does a model that is too large end up with higher loss?
options: Because larger models are more prone to overfit the test set
Because compute is fixed, a larger model trains on fewer tokens and is undertrained
Because the learning rate is too low for larger models
Because larger models have a different architecture
quiz.why: Compute ≈ 6ND is fixed, so if N increases, D must decrease in proportion. The model has more capacity but sees too little data; the "undertraining" loss rises quickly and outweighs the benefit of extra capacity. In these experiments every data point is seen only once, so there is no memorizing the test set.

sections.h: Method 3: decompose loss into three terms and solve directly

blocks.p: The third method pools all the experimental results from the first two methods and fits a formula with explicit meaning:

parts.desc: The entropy of the data itself: even with a perfect model and infinite data, this loss cannot be removed. Language itself is uncertain.
Loss caused by the model being too small: a transformer with N parameters, even trained perfectly, still falls this far short of the ideal model.
Loss caused by not training enough: the model has only seen D tokens, each once, and is this far from perfect training.
Two exponents, determining how quickly adding parameters and adding data pay off.

formula.note: The fit uses the outlier-insensitive Huber loss (δ = 10^{-3}) and the L-BFGS optimizer, choosing the best from a set of initial values to avoid local optima. The paper says that if δ were larger, the fit would over-accommodate the small-compute experiments and predict large-scale experiments worse.

plain.title: Three reasons the model can't reach a perfect score
plain.text: Break the loss into three pieces: E is the irreducible uncertainty of the task itself, which no one can remove (gray; it is actually much larger than drawn). A / N^α is "not enough brain" — the larger the model, the smaller it gets. B / D^β is "not enough reading" — the more data, the smaller it gets. The optimal allocation makes the last two pieces together as small as possible.

blocks.p: These three terms come from a classic decomposition: total loss = ideal lower bound + gap from "limited model capacity" + gap from "imperfect training." With this formula, you can compute the predicted loss for the two models by hand:

fig.title: By the formula: with the same compute, Chinchilla's predicted loss is lower
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: computed by us from the fitted formula in Appendix D.2, not measured data. Blue column is total predicted loss.
fig.note: For Gopher, the "model capacity" term is already small at 0.052, so adding more parameters yields little. But the "undertraining" term is as high as 0.251. Chinchilla shifts part of the budget from parameters to data: the first term rises by only 0.03, while the second shrinks by almost 0.09.

blocks.p: **The optimality condition**. Minimizing the loss with compute fixed at 6ND yields a neat result: at the optimum, the ratio of the two reducible losses equals β : α, i.e. A/N^{α} : B/D^{β} = 0.28 : 0.34. In plain terms: **the next unit of compute spent on more parameters must reduce loss by exactly as much as the same compute spent on more data**; otherwise, shift it to whichever has the higher return. From this the optimal exponents follow directly:

formula.expr: N_{opt} ∝ C^{a}, D_{opt} ∝ C^{b},  a = β / (α + β),  b = α / (α + β)

parts.desc: Exponent for how optimal model size grows with compute
Exponent for how optimal data volume grows with compute. a + b = 1 because N × D is proportional to compute.
The two exponents are similar, so a and b are both close to 0.5: model and data grow together.

formula.note: The paper reports Method 3 gives a = 0.46 and b = 0.54, and predicts the optimal model under Gopher's compute is about 40B parameters. Using the paper's rounded parameters gives a = 0.28 / 0.62 ≈ 0.45 (see "the parts that don't add up" below).

plain.title: Split the extra compute down the middle
plain.text: The two terms "model too small" and "data too little" shrink at similar rates with scale, as α and β are close. So extra compute should also be split roughly evenly: however much the model grows, data grows by the same factor. That is what exponents a and b near 0.5 mean.

blocks.p: As an aside, E = 1.69 is very close to the language entropy of about 1.7 nats guessed in the previous paper. But the two papers use different datasets and tokenization, so the values cannot be compared directly — it is only an interesting coincidence.

quiz.q: In L(N, D) = E + A/N^{α} + B/D^{β}, which term cannot be removed no matter how much model and data are added?
options: A/N^{α}
B/D^{β}
E
All three terms can be removed
quiz.why: E represents the uncertainty of the text itself: the same context can be followed by many reasonable words, and no amount of model scaling or data can remove it. A/N^{α} tends to 0 as the model grows; B/D^{β} tends to 0 as the data grows.

quiz.q: At the optimal allocation, why must the marginal loss reduction from adding parameters equal that from adding data?
options: Because the formula requires α = β
If one side offers a higher return, moving a little compute from the lower-return side to the other will lower total loss, so the original allocation was not optimal
Because parameters and data have the same unit cost
Because 6ND is a constant
quiz.why: This is the general principle of all budget-allocation problems: as long as two ways of spending have different marginal returns, there is room to improve until the two are equal. α and β are not equal (0.34 and 0.28), so at the optimum the ratio of the two loss terms is β : α, not 1 : 1.

sections.h: Three methods, one conclusion: model size and data grow together

fig.title: All three methods find a ≈ b ≈ 0.5, far from the old conclusion
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Table 2; values in parentheses are bootstrap-estimated 10% and 90% percentiles. Blue column is the data exponent b.
rows: Method 1: lower envelope of training curves
fig.note: The paper also re-ran Method 2 on two other datasets, C4 and GitHub code, getting 0.50 / 0.50 and 0.53 / 0.47, respectively — same conclusion.

blocks.p: The three methods used different fitting procedures and different models, yet reached nearly the same conclusion. Method 3 predicts a somewhat smaller optimal model; the paper explains that its Huber loss automatically treats small-compute experiments as outliers and gives more weight to large-compute points, and that the compute-to-optimal-model-size relationship curves slightly downward at large scale.

**About 20 tokens per parameter**. The paper's Table 3 lists, from Method 1, how much data models of different sizes need to be compute-optimal: 1B parameters needs about 20.2B tokens, 10B needs about 205.1B, and 67B needs about 1.5T. The ratios all come out around 20 (this rule of thumb is computed by us from the table; the paper's main text does not state it this way).

fig.title: How much data and compute a model needs to be compute-optimal
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Table 3 (Method 1). "Tokens per parameter" is computed by us; "Gopher units" means the multiple of compute used to train Gopher. Amber marks the optimum at Gopher's compute budget.

blocks.p: The table's implication is sharp: a 175B-parameter model needs several trillion tokens to be worth the compute, and GPT-3 used only 300B. Training a compute-optimal 1T-parameter model is not worthwhile unless you have more than 250× the compute used for Gopher. The paper emphasizes that **larger, higher-quality datasets** will be key to further scaling language models.

quiz.q: According to the "about 20 tokens per parameter" rule of thumb, about how many tokens should a 7B-parameter model train on to be compute-optimal?
options: About 7B
About 140B
About 1.4T
About 300B
quiz.why: 7B × 20 = 140B tokens. About 1.4T is the data volume of Chinchilla (a 70B-parameter model); about 300B was the "standard" training volume for large models at the time. Later, many 7B-class models were actually trained on far more than 140B tokens; see the end of the article for why.

sections.h: Validation: training Chinchilla with Gopher's compute budget

blocks.p: According to the three methods, the optimal model under Gopher's compute budget is between 40B and 70B parameters. For dataset and computational-efficiency reasons, the authors chose the upper end: **70B parameters and 1.4T tokens**, using the same compute as Gopher.

fig.title: Chinchilla and Gopher: same depth, half the width
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Table 4; batch size doubles partway through training. Amber is Chinchilla.

plain.title: Same compute, split differently
plain.text: Gopher was 280B parameters and read only 300B tokens; Chinchilla shrank the model to 70B and increased the reading to 1.4T tokens. The compute is similar, yet the latter is better on almost all tasks and cheaper to run.

blocks.p: Beyond size and data volume, the two models differ in several other ways, all listed in the paper:

list: **Data mix**: both use the MassiveText dataset, but because more tokens are needed, the sampling proportions of subsets were adjusted slightly; the web and Wikipedia portions are seen more than once.
**Optimizer**: Chinchilla uses AdamW; Gopher used Adam. The paper finds that AdamW improves language-modeling loss and downstream performance.
**Tokenizer**: it removes a text-normalization step (NFKC); the vocabulary is 94.15% identical to Gopher's, which helps with representing math and chemistry symbols.
**Numerical precision**: forward and backward passes use bfloat16, but a float32 copy of the weights is kept in the optimizer state.

callout.title: This is not a controlled experiment that changes only one variable.
callout.text: The optimizer, tokenizer, and precision differences could all make Chinchilla stronger. In the appendix, the paper compares Adam and AdamW separately and confirms AdamW is better on its own. Strictly speaking, then, part of Chinchilla's margin over Gopher cannot be attributed to better compute allocation. The paper also ran a cleaner small-scale comparison: at 10^{21} FLOPs, the old method recommended 4.68B parameters and the new method 2.86B; trained with identical settings, the new method's model performed better.

sections.h: Results: beats Gopher on almost all benchmarks

blocks.p: The paper compares Chinchilla with Gopher, GPT-3, MT-NLG 530B, and other models on a wide range of tasks: language modeling, reading comprehension, question answering, commonsense reasoning, MMLU, BIG-bench, and more. The most closely watched is MMLU, an exam-style benchmark covering 57 subjects:

fig.title: MMLU 5-shot average accuracy: 70B-parameter Chinchilla passes 60% for the first time
fig.subtitle: Units: %. From the paper's Table 6. Amber is Chinchilla; "2023 forecast" is the average forecast made in 2021 by professional forecasters for the best result by June 2023.

blocks.p: Chinchilla scores 7.6 points higher than Gopher, even exceeding forecasters' average expectation for June 2023. Across the 57 subjects, it is better on 51, tied on 2, and worse on only 4 (college mathematics, econometrics, moral scenarios, formal logic).

fig.title: Other representative tasks: mostly clear wins
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Tables 7–9 and main text; units: accuracy %. Blue column is Chinchilla.
fig.note: On the commonsense benchmark PIQA, both models score 81.8%. On RACE, GPT-3 and MT-NLG used different prompt formats, so the paper notes these numbers cannot be compared directly.

blocks.p: Two details worth noting. First, Chinchilla also leads comprehensively on language-modeling tests such as The Pile, but the paper cautions that it saw 4× more data, so the risk of test-set content leaking into training is greater; it therefore weights MMLU, BIG-bench, and similarly leak-resistant tasks more. Second, zero-shot TruthfulQA improved by 14.1 points. Earlier work had suggested larger models become less truthful; the paper argues that **merely learning the pretraining data better** can clearly improve truthfulness.

**Bias and toxicity.** On Winogender (which tests whether pronoun resolution is affected by gender stereotypes), Chinchilla is more accurate than Gopher in every group, but male pronouns improve by only 3.2 points, while female and neutral pronouns improve by 8.3 and 9.2 points respectively — so the gains are uneven. On toxicity, the average toxicity score over 25,000 unprompted generations is 0.087, versus 0.081 for Gopher; the difference is negligible. A better language model is not necessarily more toxic, nor necessarily less toxic.

sections.h: Where the paper doesn't add up

blocks.p: The paper's conclusions are solid, but many details contain numbers that contradict each other. Here they are one by one, worth watching for when reading the original:

list: **MMLU score**: the abstract says 67.5% and "more than 7 percentage points"; the main text and Table 6 say 67.6% and 7.6 points higher.

**Compute and data for a 175B-parameter model**: the main text says 4.41 × 10^{24} FLOPs and over 4.2T tokens, but Table 3, which the text cites, says 3.85 × 10^{24} and 3.7T. For a 280B-parameter model, the main text says about 10^{25} FLOPs and 6.8T tokens, while Table 3 says 9.90 × 10^{24} and 5.9T. The main-text numbers also disagree with the Method 2 and Method 3 tables in the appendix.

**Appendix Table A3 appears to be off by an order of magnitude**: in the Method 3 column, the compute for the 175B-parameter model is written as 1.26 × 10^{24}, smaller than the 1.71 × 10^{24} for the previous row, 67B parameters. Checking with 6ND: 175B parameters × 12T tokens × 6 ≈ 1.26 × 10^{25}, so this is likely a typo.

**Method 3 exponents**: Table 2 gives a = 0.46, but the 10%–90% interval in parentheses is (0.454, 0.455), so the point estimate lies outside its own interval. Using the paper's α = 0.34 and β = 0.28 gives a = 0.28 / 0.62 ≈ 0.45, which matches the interval.
**Training data range**: the abstract says models were trained on 5B to 500B tokens; the introduction says 5B to over 400B.
**GPT-3 size**: the discussion section writes GPT-3 as 170B parameters; everywhere else in the paper it is 175B.
**Gopher compute**: the main text uses the old figure of 5.76 × 10^{23}; the appendix uses a more precise calculation and gets 6.3 × 10^{23}.

callout.title: Later, researchers went back and checked the paper
callout.text: In 2024, Epoch AI researchers tried to reproduce Method 3 and pointed out that the parameters reported in the original paper were inconsistent with the first two methods, and that the confidence intervals were implausibly narrow. This is the same kind of problem as the a-value and interval mismatch above. But the core conclusions of Methods 1 and 2 — that model and data grow in roughly equal proportions — remain widely accepted.

blocks.p: Limitations the paper itself lists:

list: **Large-scale validation is only one pair**: because of cost, only Chinchilla versus Gopher can be compared at large scale; there is no further validation at intermediate sizes.
**Power-law assumption**: the observed optimal model size curves slightly downward at large compute, which means the paper may still overestimate the optimal model size at large compute.
**Data seen only once**: all experiments train for less than one epoch (data is not repeated); multi-epoch training was not studied.

**Data quality**: the paper speculates that scaling data helps only if the data is high quality; trillions of web tokens contain more toxic content, bias, and private information, and test-set leakage is harder to audit.

blocks.p: **What happened next.** Chinchilla's conclusions were quickly adopted by the industry, but a new consideration followed: **inference cost**. In February 2023, Meta released LLaMA; the paper starts by noting that Chinchilla's objective considered only the training budget and ignored the inference budget — if a model is to be deployed at scale, a smaller model trained longer is ultimately cheaper. Under Chinchilla's advice, a 10B-parameter model would need only 200B tokens, but LLaMA found that a 7B-parameter model was still improving after 1T tokens. From then on, training small models far beyond the compute-optimal point became the norm for open models.

So Chinchilla answers "what is optimal when the training budget is fixed," while the real world also includes the cost of running the model countless times. Understanding that distinction is key to understanding today's "small but strong" models.

sections.h: Quiz: did you really get it?

quiz.q: Kaplan concluded N ∝ C^{0.73}; Chinchilla concluded N ∝ C^{0.5}. If compute increases 100×, how many times larger does the optimal model become under each conclusion?
options: About 29× and 10×
About 73× and 50×
About 100× and 100×
About 5× and 3×
quiz.why: 100^{0.73} ≈ 29, and 100^{0.5} = 10. Under Chinchilla, the remaining 10× goes to more data; under Kaplan, data increases only about 100^{0.27} ≈ 3.5×. The exponent isn't a multiplier — you have to raise the increase to that power.

quiz.q: Why did the Chinchilla authors think MMLU and BIG-bench were more informative than language-modeling results on The Pile?
options: Because The Pile is too easy
Because Chinchilla saw 4× more data, so test content is more likely to have leaked into the training data, and language-modeling scores may be inflated
Because Gopher was not evaluated on The Pile
Because MMLU has more questions
quiz.why: The more data, the more likely the training set contains the same text as the test set, inflating language-modeling scores through memorization. Exam-style tasks are less affected by this kind of leakage, so the paper weights them more heavily. This is a warning the paper itself gives in the main text.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer:

list: How do Chinchilla and Kaplan differ, and what is the main source of the difference?
Why does measuring mid-training loss with a schedule designed for a long training run underestimate training on less data?
How do the three methods estimate the optimal allocation? Why is the IsoFLOP curve a valley?
In L(N, D) = E + A/N^{α} + B/D^{β}, what do the three terms represent?
At the optimal allocation, why is the ratio of the two reducible losses β : α?
Where does "about 20 tokens per parameter" come from, and under what conditions does it hold?
In Chinchilla beating Gopher, which factors cannot be attributed to compute allocation?
Why did later LLaMA deliberately train longer than "compute-optimal"?
